summary: Describes extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol for setting up point-to-multipoint and multipoint-to-multipoint label switched paths in MPLS networks, known as multipoint LDP. It builds these paths without relying on any other multicast tree protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6388 extends LDP so MPLS routers can build paths from one sender to many receivers or from many senders to many receivers. The routers build the forwarding tree by exchanging label messages through LDP.

questions: difference between p2mp and mp2mp lsp
what is make before break in mldp
subtitle: LDP extensions for building one-to-many and many-to-many label-switched paths.

tldr.problem: Base LDP supports point-to-point and multipoint-to-point paths, but not point-to-multipoint or multipoint-to-multipoint paths.
tldr.mechanism: Leaves send label mappings toward the root using new FEC elements. Transit routers install forwarding state and propagate mappings so packets are copied along branches of the path.
tldr.outcome: Multipoint LDP builds P2MP and MP2MP paths without relying on another multicast tree protocol. RFC 6388 was updated by RFC 7358.

today: RFC 6388 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7358. Read the update with this multipoint LDP specification.

sections.title: Multipoint Paths with LDP
sections.content:
Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) originally defined setup for point-to-point and multipoint-to-point Label Switched Paths (LSPs). This RFC adds point-to-multipoint (P2MP) and multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) LSPs, called multipoint LSPs.

A P2MP LSP carries traffic from one root to multiple leaves. An MP2MP LSP carries traffic from multiple ingress nodes to multiple egress nodes. A router sends one packet copy to each LDP neighbor used by the path, with replication where the path branches. The solution does not depend on another multicast tree protocol.

The leaves are assumed to know the root and LSP identifier. How they learn those values, and how applications use the LSP, are outside this document.
sections.plainLanguage: LDP can build a forwarding path that reaches multiple receivers from one root, or connects multiple senders and receivers. Routers exchange labels to create the branches.

sections.title: Roles in a Multipoint LSP
sections.content:
The root is the node whose address identifies the multipoint path. A leaf is an egress node for a P2MP LSP; an MP2MP leaf can be both ingress and egress. A transit Label Switching Router (LSR) has an upstream neighbor toward the root and one or more downstream neighbors.

A bud LSR is an egress that also has downstream neighbors. A root or transit router can also act as a leaf. The RFC notes that an FEC element identifies the multipoint LSP, but does not necessarily identify the traffic mapped to it.

Each path is identified by the root address and an opaque value. The opaque value is meaningful to ingress and leaf routers but need not be interpreted by transit routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The root identifies the path, leaves receive traffic, and transit routers connect the branches. A router may have more than one of these roles in the same path.

sections.title: FEC Elements and Capability Exchange
sections.content:
The P2MP FEC element carries an address family, root address, and opaque value. Together, the root address and opaque value uniquely identify the P2MP LSP. The FEC type is 0x06; the IPv4 root address length is 4 octets and the IPv6 length is 16 octets.

MP2MP uses downstream FEC type 0x08 and upstream FEC type 0x07. Each FEC element must be the only FEC element in its FEC TLV. The generic LSP identifier is an opaque-value element with type 1 and a 4-octet value unique in the context of the root.

Routers advertise support in the LDP Initialization message. Capability values are 0x0508 for P2MP, 0x0509 for MP2MP, and 0x050A for Make Before Break. Label messages using these FEC elements should not be sent to peers that have not advertised the corresponding capability.
sections.plainLanguage: A root address and opaque value identify each multipoint path. Before a router sends setup messages for a path type, it checks that its neighbor advertised support for that type.

sections.title: Building a P2MP LSP
sections.content:
A leaf selects its upstream LSR as the next hop on the best route to the root. It allocates a label and sends a Label Mapping upstream. A transit LSR selects its own upstream neighbor, allocates another label, installs forwarding state to swap labels toward downstream neighbors, and propagates a mapping toward the root.

If a transit router already has state for the path, it adds a new downstream branch rather than sending a duplicate mapping upstream. The root installs state to push the received label onto traffic intended for the path. The way a node chooses which traffic to map is outside the scope of the RFC.

When a leaf no longer needs the path, it can withdraw its label. A transit router removes the corresponding forwarding state and propagates the withdrawal upstream when no state remains. If the upstream LSR changes, the router replaces its label and updates the mapping and withdrawal messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Setup begins at a leaf and moves toward the root. Each router adds forwarding state and passes a label mapping upstream; routers with multiple downstream branches share the path state.

sections.title: Building an MP2MP LSP
sections.content:
An MP2MP LSP has a downstream path, similar to P2MP, and an upstream path that carries traffic toward the root and other leaves. A packet received from a downstream node must not be sent back to that same node. As a result, a leaf that sends traffic does not receive its own packets.

Leaves send MP2MP downstream Label Mappings and receive MP2MP upstream mappings. The RFC recommends ordered mode for setting up the upstream path: a router waits until the path from itself to the root is established before completing the path toward its downstream neighbor. This helps ensure that traffic sent by a leaf can reach the root rather than being dropped while setup is incomplete.

Transit and root routers build upstream forwarding state from downstream state while omitting the branch back to the sender. Withdrawals remove state in both directions.
sections.plainLanguage: MP2MP carries traffic both toward the root and back down to other leaves. Routers omit the sender's own branch so its packets do not return to it.

sections.title: Root Redundancy and Make Before Break
sections.content:
The root is a single point of failure, so the RFC describes building a tree to multiple root addresses for the same opaque value. For P2MP, only one root should forward at a time to limit bandwidth use and avoid duplicate packets. For MP2MP, each sending leaf selects one root, while all leaves join all roots. This can speed recovery but uses additional label resources.

On a LAN, upstream label allocation can reduce packet replication by using a context label to identify the upstream LSR and a second label for the LSP. The RFC also describes micro-loops: two-router loops are prevented, but loops involving more than two LSRs may occur until unicast routing converges.

Optional Make Before Break (MBB) procedures establish a new path before removing the old one. An MBB Label Mapping carries status code 1 for a request; a notification carries code 2 for acknowledgment. The old label remains active until the new upstream path reports that it is connected.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can prepare paths to backup roots and switch when needed, at the cost of extra labels. MBB keeps the old path active until the replacement path is ready.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for base LDP also apply. This specification does not provide an authorization mechanism to control which LSRs may join a multipoint LSP.

If an operator needs to restrict membership, additional mechanisms outside this document are required. The root alone cannot enforce such a policy because it does not learn the identities of all leaf nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: This protocol does not decide which routers are allowed to join a multipoint path. Any membership restrictions need other mechanisms, and cannot be enforced only at the root.
